meta.subtitle: Automated semiconductor-test and robotics maker in a memory-driven AI-test upcycle; a net-cash balance sheet against a rich, cyclical-peak multiple.

analystSentiment.commentary: The Street is constructive but not euphoric. Across 17 analysts the split is 12 Buy, 5 Hold and 0 Sell, a consensus of Buy. The consensus price target is $446.47, {+ +12.0% +} above the $398.69 quote, with a median of $450.00 and a range from $350.00 to $550.00. The implied upside is narrow for a Buy consensus, and the five Holds capture the tension in the name: the operating momentum is not in doubt, but the valuation already discounts much of it. Where our own view sits relative to that consensus is set out in the valuation section.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Teradyne, Inc. designs and manufactures automated test equipment for semiconductors and advanced robotics systems. It reports three groups: Semiconductor Test — its core — which tests wafers and packaged devices across compute, memory, automotive and communications on the FLEX, J750, Magnum and ETS platforms; Product Test, covering defense and aerospace, circuit-board and wireless test; and Robotics, its collaborative and mobile robots. Teradyne sells to integrated device manufacturers, fabless chip designers, foundries and assembly-and-test subcontractors, and has a strategic collaboration with Tokyo Electron Limited to develop a test-cell solution for AI and data-center device screening. The company was incorporated in 1960 and is headquartered in North Reading, Massachusetts. FY25 revenue was $3.2B, up {+ +13.1% +}, with net income of $554M and GAAP diluted EPS of $3.47.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: Teradyne is a direct beneficiary of the AI build-out's demand for semiconductor test: second-quarter revenue reached $1.3B, up {+ 104% +} year over year, on memory-test strength from DRAM and a NAND final-test resurgence. Consensus has revenue and earnings rising steeply into FY27. The balance sheet is net cash, and the company returns most of its free cash flow to shareholders. The counter-case is the cycle and the price: automated test is a cyclical capital-equipment business — Teradyne's own revenue fell from $3.7B in FY21 to $2.7B in FY23 — and at 54.8x trailing earnings the shares price in sustained peak demand. We rate the shares HOLD: the growth is real, but the reward is modest against a real cyclical downside.

catalysts: Memory-test strength: second-quarter memory revenue rose on DRAM demand and a NAND final-test resurgence, the clearest driver of the current upcycle.
AI and data-center test: the Tokyo Electron collaboration targets a test-cell solution for screening AI and data-center devices at the leading edge.
The 2027 outlook: management points to a rising wafer-fab-equipment investment cycle sustaining growth beyond the current year.
Capital returns: Teradyne returns most of its cash to shareholders, chiefly through buybacks, backed by a net-cash balance sheet.
risks: Cyclicality: automated test is tied to the lumpy wafer-fab-equipment and memory cycles; Teradyne's revenue fell in both FY22 and FY23.
Sequential deceleration: third-quarter revenue and EPS are guided below the second quarter, an early sign the current pace is moderating.
Valuation: the rich trailing multiple leaves little room if the earnings ramp stalls or the multiple compresses.
Customer and end-market concentration: demand hinges on a handful of large chipmakers' capital spending, especially in memory and AI compute.
Trade and export controls: tariffs and U.S.–China semiconductor export rules can restrict sales to affected customers.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue is cyclical and has just inflected sharply. Across FY21–FY25 revenue moved from $3.7B to $3.2B with a trough of $2.7B in FY23, while operating margin ranged from 32.4% down to 18.7% and back to 20.4%; gross margin held near 58% throughout. GAAP diluted EPS fell from $5.53 in FY21 to $2.73 in FY23 before recovering to $3.47 in FY25. The second quarter of 2026 broke the pattern: revenue of $1.3B rose {+ 104% +} year over year and operating margin reached 32.9%, with GAAP EPS of $2.38 and non-GAAP EPS of $2.47. By group, Semiconductor Test contributed $1,122 million of the quarter, Product Test $107 million and Robotics $100 million, so the test franchise, led by memory, is carrying the upcycle. The gap between GAAP and non-GAAP is small here.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: The balance sheet is a source of strength through the cycle. Teradyne ended FY25 in a net-cash position, with net debt of -$93.8M against just $200M of total debt and $2.8B of equity. Trailing interest coverage is 118.8x and net debt to EBITDA is -0.2x, so leverage is not a concern. The current ratio was 1.75 at year-end 2025 and 2.12 on a trailing basis. That financial flexibility lets the company keep investing and returning capital across the semiconductor cycle's swings rather than being forced to retrench at the bottom.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation is steady and returned aggressively. FY25 operating cash flow was $674.4 million and free cash flow was $450 million, a 14.1% FCF margin, on light capital expenditure of about $224 million. Teradyne returned $785 million to shareholders in 2025 — 116% of operating cash flow and 174% of free cash flow — through $702.1 million of buybacks and $76.3 million of dividends. The dividend yields just 0.14%, so repurchases are the main return channel. Returning more than free cash flow is sustainable only while the net-cash balance sheet and the current earnings level hold; a cyclical downturn would tighten that math.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: Teradyne trades at a premium that assumes the upcycle endures. The shares are at 54.8x trailing earnings, 14.0x sales and 41.8x EV/EBITDA. The forward multiple falls as estimates rise — 43.9x on next-twelve-month earnings and about 34.2x on the FY27E consensus EPS — but those forward figures rest on the earnings ramp holding through a notoriously cyclical end market. Peer multiples are pending a peer data source, so we anchor on what the company's own multiple implies: the market is paying for the current earnings level to persist, which leaves little margin for a memory or wafer-fab-equipment air pocket.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The AI-test upcycle sustains through 2027, memory-test demand stays strong, the wafer-fab-equipment investment cycle keeps building, and Teradyne beats the FY27E EPS of $11.65 while holding a premium multiple on a larger earnings base.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Revenue lands near the consensus path, growth decelerates from the second quarter's pace, and the forward multiple normalizes modestly as the market discounts the cyclical nature of the earnings.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: The memory and wafer-fab-equipment cycle rolls over, the earnings ramp stalls short of the FY27E path, and the rich trailing multiple compresses sharply on lower earnings — the pattern Teradyne's own FY22–FY23 downturn showed.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: Weighting the three cases gives a fair value about {+ +2.9% +} above the current price, against a bear case {- -28.5% -} below it, for a reward/risk of 0.10x. That is a HOLD: the expected upside is slim and the downside, driven by the cycle and the multiple together, is large. Our weighted fair value of about $410 sits below the Street's $446.47 consensus target — we share the constructive read on the franchise but are less willing to pay a peak multiple for peak-cyclical earnings. The target range of $360 to $500 straddles the current price, reflecting a name whose next move depends more on the cycle than on execution.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Teradyne reports as a single segment for the structured mix, but the business is three groups. Semiconductor Test dominates — $1,122 million of second-quarter revenue — and is where the moat is strongest: automated test equipment is co-developed with chipmakers years ahead of a device's ramp, qualified into the customer's manufacturing flow, and supported for the product's life, which raises switching costs and narrows the field to a few credible suppliers. Product Test ($107 million) serves defense, circuit-board and wireless test, and Robotics ($100 million) sells collaborative and mobile robots into a more competitive, lower-margin market. The Magnum memory-test platform and the Tokyo Electron collaboration position the test franchise at the leading edge of AI and memory, where the current demand is concentrated.

moatFactors.name: Co-development and qualification
moatFactors.body: Test programs are developed alongside chipmakers well before a device ships and qualified into the customer's manufacturing flow, so switching suppliers mid-cycle is costly and rare.

moatFactors.name: Installed base and support
moatFactors.body: A large installed base of test systems generates recurring service, spares and software revenue and keeps Teradyne embedded in customers' operations across product generations.

moatFactors.name: Leading-edge positioning
moatFactors.body: The Magnum memory platform and the Tokyo Electron AI and data-center collaboration place the test franchise where demand is concentrated, in memory and AI compute.

moatFactors.name: Cyclicality and competition
moatFactors.body: Automated test is a cyclical capital-equipment market with a small number of strong competitors, and the Robotics group competes in a more crowded, lower-margin field — both cap the width of the moat.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is real but narrow, and it is wrapped around a cyclical core. Its durability rests on the co-development relationships and the installed base, which persist across cycles even as revenue swings. Working against it is the demand pattern: test-equipment orders track customers' capital spending, which is lumpy and periodic. Teradyne's own history — revenue falling in FY22 and FY23 before this upcycle — shows the franchise endures downturns but its earnings do not. The durability question is therefore less about competitive position, which is secure, than about how far and how fast the current demand normalizes.

points: Consensus sees revenue reaching about $5.1B in FY26, up {+ 61% +}, and $6.3B in FY27, with EPS climbing to $9.09 then $11.65 — a steep ramp off the FY25 base.
Operating leverage is high: gross margin runs near 58–60%, so the second quarter's revenue surge lifted operating margin sharply, and incremental revenue converts efficiently to profit.
Semiconductor Test, the core group, grew revenue about 19% in FY25 on AI-related demand in compute, networking and memory, ahead of the total company.
Robotics returned to growth through 2025 and could add a second engine if the recovery proves durable.
The growth is cyclical, not secular: the operating leverage that lifts margins in the upcycle reverses in a downturn, and the FY26–FY27 ramp assumes the memory cycle does not roll over.

management.leadership: Gregory S. Smith is President and Chief Executive Officer. Michelle Turner became Vice President, Chief Financial Officer and Treasurer on November 3, 2025, succeeding Sanjay Mehta. The named-executive group also includes the General Counsel and the presidents of the Semiconductor Test and Product Test groups, several of whom stepped into their roles in 2025 — Shannon Poulin as President, Semiconductor Test in April 2025 and Regan Mills as President, Product Test in March 2025. The recent CFO and group-president transitions are the main continuity item to watch, though the turnover has coincided with the company's strongest operating results.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation favors shareholder returns and bolt-on M&A over heavy internal capital. Teradyne does not own fabs, so capital expenditure is light and free cash flow is high relative to revenue; management returned well over 100% of it in a strong year through buybacks and a small dividend. The company has also used acquisitions to extend the portfolio, integrating Quantifi Photonics into Product Test and holding an investment in Technoprobe. The approach suits a cyclical business with a net-cash balance sheet: return cash when earnings are high, keep the flexibility to invest through a downturn. The risk is repurchasing stock near a cyclical and valuation peak.
management.governance: Governance is straightforward for a large-cap. The board is majority independent under Nasdaq standards; the proxy identifies nine directors it determined independent for fiscal 2025 — one of whom, Ford Tamer, resigned effective May 9, 2025 — and discloses that several of them serve on the boards of Teradyne customers or suppliers — Analog Devices, Synopsys, Sandisk and others — with the board judging none of those relationships material enough to impair independence. Related-party transactions above the $120,000 threshold are reviewed by the Audit Committee under a written policy, and the proxy states there have been no disclosable related-person transactions since January 1, 2025. Nothing in the governance disclosure stands out as a concern.

idiosyncratic: Cyclicality of test demand: orders track customers' wafer-fab-equipment and memory capital spending, which is lumpy and periodic; Teradyne's revenue fell in both FY22 and FY23, and the memory portion driving the current upcycle is the most cyclical part of the mix.

Peak-earnings valuation: the forward multiples rest on the FY26–FY27 earnings ramp holding; if that ramp stalls, earnings can fall as they did in the prior downturn, and a high multiple on lower earnings compounds the move.
Customer concentration: a handful of large chipmakers and their capital-spending decisions drive a disproportionate share of demand, so a pause by one large customer can swing results.
Robotics execution: the Robotics group operates in a more competitive, lower-margin market and has needed restructuring; its recovery is not assured.
Trade and export controls: U.S.–China export rules and tariffs can restrict sales to affected customers and disrupt the supply chain.
risks.systemic: Teradyne's fortunes are tied to the global semiconductor capital-equipment cycle, which is itself driven by end demand for chips and by a small number of large customers' investment plans. A broad slowdown in technology capital spending, a downturn in the memory market, or an escalation of U.S.–China trade and export restrictions would each hit demand, and the effects tend to arrive together and quickly in this industry. Because the shares carry a high multiple on cyclically elevated earnings, a systemic shock would likely compress the valuation and the earnings at the same time — the classic risk of owning a cyclical at a peak.

body: We rate Teradyne HOLD with a target range of $360 to $500. The operating story is strong: second-quarter revenue rose sharply on memory-test demand, the balance sheet is net cash, and the company converts revenue to cash and returns it to shareholders. Consensus has earnings climbing steeply into FY27, and the franchise's co-development moat is secure.

What holds us at HOLD is the combination of a cyclical business and a peak multiple. Teradyne's own history shows revenue and earnings fall in downturns, third-quarter guidance already steps down sequentially, and the shares discount much of the good news — so the reward/risk we set out in the valuation section is skewed to the downside, and our fair value sits below the Street's.

We would turn more positive if the shares de-rated toward a normalized multiple or if demand broadened durably beyond memory; we would turn cautious if the memory cycle or wafer-fab-equipment spending rolled over. For now the quality is not in question, but the price already reflects it — a HOLD that respects both the franchise and the cycle.
